case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: The Court stressed the platforms' passivity and distance from the wrongdoers. A provider that fine-tunes, moderates in real time, or profits from a specific user relationship is less passive, and the opinion leaves that door visibly open.
case.holding: Platforms whose recommendation algorithms treated terrorist content like any other content did not aid and abet terrorism. Generalised, passive assistance through generally available infrastructure is not culpable participation.
case.why_ai_cites_it: The strongest recent authority that operating a neutral algorithmic system at scale is not complicity in what users do with it. AI providers cite its framing, arms-length provision of a widely available tool, against secondary-liability theories for downstream misuse of models and agents.

reading.body:
Twitter v. Taamneh is cited by the defense, and its holding that passive, generally available algorithmic infrastructure is not complicity in what users do with it is invoked in four active lawsuits, all against Character Technologies.

That the same precedent recurs across four separate Character Technologies cases suggests defendants view algorithmic-neutrality reasoning as their strongest available argument for that specific category of claim, chatbot companion products where a user's own interactions shape what the system produces. The Supreme Court's own limits on the holding matter here. It stressed the platforms' passivity, and a product that fine-tunes or moderates in real time is less passive, which the case record leaves as an open question for how far this defense actually reaches.

The data does not resolve whether that open question has been decided in any of the four cases citing it, only that the precedent is in active use as of the case's most recent verification.

section.name: AI Case Law: The Precedents Behind the Defenses
